--- title: "Player impact from lineups" --- ::: {#takeaways .cell execution_count=1} ::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"} ## Takeaways - **Lineups rebuilt for every game since 2003-04 (NBA) and 2009 (WNBA).** In every season they account for at least 95% of points and possessions (98-100% in most). - **Player impact predicts next season better than the team's own results.** Last season's player impact, weighted by who actually plays this season, explains 50% of next-season NBA team net rating (36% WNBA), against 35% (24% WNBA) for the team's own net rating last season. - **Net rating plus our variables predicts playoff series better than net rating alone.** Adding availability-adjusted strength (this season's player impact, counting only players available for the playoffs) improves NBA series predictions (+0.020 log-likelihood per series, one-sided p = 0.04); in the WNBA the gain points the same way (p = 0.04). Details on the Championships page. - **Weighting the archetype mix by player quality did not beat quality alone.** Who is good matters more than which role they play. ::: ::: ## The model we settled on, and why | league | model | series called correctly | avg chance on eventual champion | champion in top 3 | gain over net rating (p) | |:---------|:-------------------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------|:----------------------------------|:--------------------|:---------------------------| | NBA | Net rating alone (baseline) | 70% | 15% | 54% | | | NBA | Availability-adjusted strength alone (ours) | 74% | 15% | 77% | p = 0.05 | | NBA | **Net rating + availability-adjusted strength (chosen)** | 74% | 18% | 69% | p = 0.04 | | NBA | Net + ours + star player | 72% | 19% | 69% | p = 0.07 | | NBA | Net + ours + star + archetype x quality | 71% | 18% | 54% | p = 0.33 | | NBA | Net + ours split offense/defense + archetype x quality + age | 71% | 15% | 69% | p = 0.36 | | WNBA | Net rating alone (baseline) | 71% | 30% | 80% | | | WNBA | Availability-adjusted strength alone (ours) | 70% | 27% | 80% | p = 0.22 | | WNBA | **Net rating + availability-adjusted strength (chosen)** | 71% | 35% | 80% | p = 0.04 | | WNBA | Net + ours + star player | 70% | 35% | 80% | p = 0.26 | | WNBA | Net + ours + star + archetype x quality | 70% | 36% | 80% | p = 0.56 | | WNBA | Net + ours split offense/defense + archetype x quality + age | 70% | 37% | 80% | p = 0.48 | **Why this one.** *Availability-adjusted strength* is our variable: each team rebuilt from this season's lineup-based player impact, counting only the players available for the playoffs, so a team that lost its best player late in the season is rated on the roster it will actually play with. Net rating can't see that. - **It beats net rating.** In the NBA it calls more playoff series correctly and puts more probability on the eventual champion; the gain over net rating alone is statistically reliable (one-sided p = 0.04). - **In the NBA, our variable carries the most weight.** In the combined NBA model it holds 51% of the weight against 49% for net rating (45% vs 55% in the WNBA). - **Why keep net rating in it.** Our variable alone is about as good at calling series but less steady at picking champions in some seasons; net rating captures things our lineup estimates miss (team scheme and coaching, and players with too few minutes to estimate well). Together they are the most accurate and the most stable in both leagues. - **Star players.** Adding the best available player's impact ("star") gives the best NBA title picker and the best series log-loss, so star power is used in the 2026-27 forecast (Jokić, Gilgeous-Alexander and Wembanyama drive their teams' ratings). It adds nothing in the WNBA, so the two-variable model stays the main one for both leagues. - **Archetype x quality.** Tuning its penalty inside the season-by-season test lifted it to about the chosen model's level (NBA ~18% on the champion, WNBA ~36%), but not above it: with 13-20 test seasons, six extra role variables add noise about as fast as signal. Who is good still explains more than which role they play. - **How it is trained.** Season by season, using only earlier seasons, with recent seasons weighted more heavily (the weighting is chosen from past seasons only). ## Other approaches we tested Everything below led to the chosen model. Roster-only versions use **last season's** player impact so that no information from the season being predicted leaks in; they show how much roster quality alone can do. ## How it is measured Every stretch of play with the same ten players on the floor (a *stint*) is one observation. A ridge regression gives each player an **offense** and a **defense** effect in points per 100 possessions, holding the other nine players fixed. The ridge penalty pulls small samples toward average, and each season starts from the player's previous-season estimate. Defense counts as much as offense here, unlike box-score measures. **Avoiding leakage:** this season's impact, summed across a roster, rebuilds this season's net rating. So every roster-based prediction below uses **last season's** player impact applied to this season's roster. ## Top players (latest two seasons) At least 800 minutes.
